44. Molecules in the Surface Layer

At the molecular scale, the boundary between a liquid and a gas is not a geometrical surface of zero thickness, but a surface layer about several molecular diameters thick.
The geometrical dividing surface used in macroscopic descriptions approximates this transition region.

The neighbors around a surface-layer molecule differ from those around a molecule inside the liquid.
An interior molecule has neighboring molecules in every direction;

for a surface-layer molecule, interactions come mainly from the liquid side.
Only when the temperature is far from the critical temperature and the vapor density is much smaller than the liquid density can this approximate model neglect the action of vapor molecules on surface-layer molecules.
This approximation must not be applied without its conditions to every liquid-gas interface.

When molecular separations are of the order of several molecular radii, attraction is important;
at very short separations, repulsion becomes important.

In the textbook surface-layer diagram, the attraction from other molecules acts overall toward the liquid interior, while a close neighboring molecule below can also exert an outward repulsive force.
Both effects must be included when discussing equilibrium.

Keeping only inward attraction would incorrectly suggest that surface molecules are always accelerating inward.
Liquid molecules continually undergo thermal motion: they can move near temporary local equilibrium positions, but their neighbors and local positions change rather than remaining permanently fixed as in a solid lattice.

When a molecule leaves the surface and enters the liquid interior, another molecule can take its place.
Macroscopic equilibrium means neither that every molecule is motionless nor that its instantaneous resultant force is always zero.

In the simplified nearest-neighbor model used by the textbook, attraction and repulsion together produce larger average molecular separations in the surface layer, and a correspondingly lower density than in the liquid interior.
This compares average structure, not every instantaneous position during thermal motion.

Molecule 2 exerts a short-range repulsive force $F_2$ on molecule 1.
The resultant attraction of the other molecules (3, 4, 5, and so on) on molecule 1 is denoted by $F_{3,4,5\ldots}$ (Figure 68).

These opposite actions describe the equilibrium of a surface molecule, not continual inward acceleration.
The resultant attraction of the other interior molecules on molecule 2 is denoted by $F_{4,5,6\ldots}$, and the repulsion exerted by molecule 3 on molecule 2 is denoted by $F_3$.

Molecule 1 also exerts the repulsive force $F_1$ on molecule 2.
The textbook model gives this order of average separations: the distance between molecules 1 and 2 is greater than that between molecules 2 and 3.

The distance between molecules 2 and 3 is greater than that between molecules 3 and 4;
farther into the liquid, the difference between the surface layer and the interior gradually decreases.



Figure 68

In this simplified model, **the average molecular separation in the surface layer is greater than in the liquid interior.**
The textbook describes this average arrangement as a surface layer in a "stretched" state.
This comparison of average molecular structure does not mean that surface molecules experience a permanent inward resultant force or that thermal motion has stopped.
